items.title: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
items.tldr: Former President Donald Trump announced plans to create an AI Force and appoint an AI tsar, pledging to accelerate U.S. AI development while dismissing safety concerns. The move signals a hard‑line stance against regulatory delays amid a global AI arms race, particularly with China.
items.background: In the wake of growing international debate over the safety and governance of large language models, Trump leveraged his social media platform to announce a new executive initiative. He framed AI as the next industrial revolution, estimating it could contribute up to 25% of U.S. GDP. The announcement came as the U.S. and China intensify competition over AI supremacy, with Beijing investing heavily in generative models and the U.S. industry grappling with calls for regulation from researchers and lawmakers.

analysis.heading: Strategic Imperatives
analysis.content: Trump’s rhetoric underscores a belief that AI is a national security asset. By creating an AI Force, the administration aims to centralize coordination across federal agencies, streamline talent acquisition, and accelerate deployment of AI in defense, intelligence, and economic sectors. The appointment of an AI tsar would grant a single point of accountability, potentially expediting policy decisions but also concentrating power in a role that could sidestep existing oversight mechanisms.

analysis.heading: Regulatory Landscape
analysis.content: The initiative arrives amid a polarized U.S. policy debate. While Trump dismisses safety concerns as a "hoax," industry leaders like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have called for a slowdown and independent monitoring. Congressional proposals for AI regulation, including mandatory kill switches and data provenance standards, face opposition from the executive branch. The AI Force could either serve as a platform for implementing voluntary industry standards or become a vehicle for preempting stricter legislation.

analysis.heading: Competitive Dynamics
analysis.content: China’s aggressive AI strategy—highlighted by state‑backed firms such as Baidu and Tencent—poses a direct challenge to U.S. dominance. Trump’s vow to keep the U.S. ahead of China signals a shift toward a more confrontational stance, potentially prompting a global AI arms race. The move may also influence international partners, encouraging allies to align with U.S. policy or to pursue independent AI pathways, thereby reshaping the geopolitical AI landscape.

key_facts: Trump announced the creation of an AI Force and the appointment of an AI tsar via a social media post.
He claims AI could account for up to 25% of U.S. GDP and is essential for maintaining a lead over China.
The initiative will rely on existing criminal and civil justice systems to target bad actors.
He dismissed safety concerns raised by researchers as a "hoax."
Industry leaders such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei have urged caution and regulatory oversight.
implications: Potential acceleration of U.S. AI development may outpace safety safeguards, increasing the risk of misuse.
items.outlook: The AI Force could become a pivotal instrument in the U.S. AI strategy, but its effectiveness will hinge on balancing rapid innovation with robust governance. If the administration adopts a collaborative approach with industry and academia, it may set a precedent for responsible AI deployment. Conversely, a unilateral, top‑down model risks alienating stakeholders and provoking international backlash, especially from allies wary of U.S. dominance in AI policy. The next few months will be critical as the executive branch outlines the structure, funding, and oversight mechanisms for the AI Force and the AI tsar, and as Congress responds to the administration’s hard‑line stance.
items.fulltext:
Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
- Published
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.
In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place.
His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development.
Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan.
- Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
  - Published3 days ago
"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI.
AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week.
Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI.
He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax".
Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks.
Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.
AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity".
Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations.
Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco.
In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.
The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.
  - Published11 September
